summary: Specifies TLS cipher suites that use the Camellia block cipher, adding versions that use newer SHA-2 hash algorithms alongside those in RFC 4132. It is a Proposed Standard and replaced RFC 4132.

plainLanguage.summary:
RFC 5932 lists the TLS cipher suites that use Camellia, a block cipher. A cipher suite is a named bundle of choices: how the two sides agree on a key, which cipher protects the data, and which hash checks that it was not altered.

The document keeps the twelve suites that RFC 4132 defined and adds twelve more whose names end in SHA256, because they check the data with HMAC-SHA-256 instead of the older HMAC-SHA1. The new suites work only with TLS 1.2 and later.

questions: which tls versions can use sha256 camellia cipher suites
subtitle: TLS cipher suites that use the Camellia block cipher, including SHA-2 based ones.

tldr.problem: TLS needed cipher suites built on the Camellia block cipher, but the original set only offered the older SHA-1 based message authentication code, so a client and server could not agree on Camellia with a SHA-2 hash.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5932 keeps the twelve cipher suites of RFC 4132 and adds twelve more that use HMAC-SHA-256 instead of HMAC-SHA1, assigning each a code in the TLS cipher suite registry. The SHA-256 suites may only be negotiated with TLS 1.2 or later.
tldr.outcome: The document is a Proposed Standard from June 2010 that obsoletes RFC 4132, and it has since been updated by RFC 10015. It reports no known weak keys and no known security problem in Camellia.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The document specifies a set of cipher suites for the Transport Layer Security protocol, as described in RFC 5246, that support the Camellia encryption algorithm as a block cipher. It adds variants that use the SHA-2 family of cryptographic hash algorithms to the set originally specified in RFC 4132, and it obsoletes RFC 4132.

The Camellia algorithm and its properties are described in RFC 3713. The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS negotiates a cipher suite before any data is sent. The suite decides the key exchange, the cipher and the hash function. Camellia was added as one more option for the cipher, and this document defines the complete set of suites that use it.

sections.title: The Cipher Suite Identifiers
sections.content:
Each cipher suite has a two byte identifier, and the document lists all of them. Six suites use Camellia with a 128-bit key and the older SHA-1 based hash, running from {0x00,0x41} for TLS_RSA_WITH_CAMELLIA_128_CBC_SHA to {0x00,0x46} for TLS_DH_anon_WITH_CAMELLIA_128_CBC_SHA. Six more use a 256-bit key with the same hash, from {0x00,0x84} to {0x00,0x89}.

The second block of twelve uses the SHA-256 based hash. The 128-bit key suites run from {0x00,0xBA} for TLS_RSA_WITH_CAMELLIA_128_CBC_SHA256 to {0x00,0xBF} for TLS_DH_anon_WITH_CAMELLIA_128_CBC_SHA256, and the 256-bit key suites from {0x00,0xC0} to {0x00,0xC5}.

The pattern in each name is the same throughout. The first part names the key exchange, the middle names Camellia and its key size, and the last part names the hash function used for message authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Each suite is identified by two bytes, and the names follow the same pattern every time: how the key is agreed, which Camellia key size is used, and which hash function checks the data.

sections.title: Key Exchange, Cipher and Hash
sections.content:
The RSA, DHE_RSA, DH_RSA, DHE_DSS, DH_DSS and DH_anon key exchanges are performed as defined in RFC 5246, so this document changes nothing about how the two sides agree on a key.

The cipher is Camellia in Cipher Block Chaining mode. The CAMELLIA_128_CBC suites use a 128-bit key and a 128-bit initialisation vector, and the CAMELLIA_256_CBC suites use a 256-bit key and a 128-bit initialisation vector.

The cipher suites whose names end in _SHA use HMAC-SHA1 as the message authentication code algorithm. When they are used with TLS versions prior to 1.2, the pseudorandom function is calculated as specified in the appropriate version of the TLS specification.

The cipher suites whose names end in _SHA256 use HMAC-SHA-256 as the message authentication code algorithm, and the pseudorandom function is the TLS PRF of RFC 5246 with SHA-256 as the hash function.
sections.plainLanguage: Only two things are new: the cipher, which is Camellia in CBC mode with a 128-bit or 256-bit key, and the hash, which is HMAC-SHA1 for the older suites and HMAC-SHA-256 for the newer ones. Everything else, including how the key is agreed, follows the TLS specification unchanged.

sections.title: The Version Rule for the SHA-256 Suites
sections.content:
The cipher suites ending in _SHA256 must not be negotiated by TLS 1.1 or earlier versions. Clients must not offer these cipher suites if they do not offer TLS 1.2 or later. Servers that select an earlier version of TLS must not select one of these cipher suites.

The rule exists because the pseudorandom function for these suites is the TLS PRF with SHA-256 as the hash function, and that construction is tied to TLS 1.2.
sections.plainLanguage: The SHA-256 suites need TLS 1.2 or later. A client running an older version must not offer them, and a server that settles on an older version must not pick one.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA updated the entries for the numbers that had been allocated in RFC 4132 to reference this document instead. Those are the six _SHA suites for a 128-bit key, from {0x00,0x41} to {0x00,0x46}, and the six for a 256-bit key, from {0x00,0x84} to {0x00,0x89}.

IANA also allocated the twelve new numbers for the SHA-256 suites: the six 128-bit key suites from {0x00,0xBA} to {0x00,0xBF}, and the six 256-bit key suites from {0x00,0xC0} to {0x00,0xC5}.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry now points the old Camellia codes at this document, and the twelve new codes for the SHA-256 suites have been handed out by IANA.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
At the time of writing, there are no known weak keys for Camellia, and no security problem had been found in Camellia, according to the NESSIE project, the Cryptography Research and Evaluation Committees and the published analysis of Camellia-128.

Security issues are discussed throughout RFC 5246, especially in its Appendices D, E and F.
sections.plainLanguage: The document reports that no weak Camellia keys are known and that no security problem had been found in the cipher. The wider questions about TLS security are covered in the TLS specification itself.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content:
This document was published in June 2010 as an Internet Standards Track document. It obsoletes RFC 4132, which had defined the original Camellia cipher suites for TLS in July 2005, and it has since been updated by RFC 10015.

The document's own scope is narrow on purpose. It defines which cipher suite identifiers exist and which TLS versions may use them; the algorithm itself is specified separately in RFC 3713, and the handshake that negotiates them is specified in RFC 5246.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 4132 was the original document for Camellia cipher suites, and this one replaced it, later amended by RFC 10015. It remains the reference for the Camellia cipher suite codes and for the rule that the SHA-256 suites need TLS 1.2.

items.title: Negotiation
items.text: The cipher suites ending in SHA256 must not be negotiated by TLS 1.1 or earlier versions.

items.title: Clients
items.text: A client that does not offer TLS 1.2 or later must not offer these cipher suites.

items.title: Servers
items.text: A server that selects an earlier version of TLS must not select one of these cipher suites.
